results.title: Listening practice Japanese – methods and drills that work
results.content:
1. Transcript-check exercise: Open MyKikitori story #12 (a 30-second beginner clip). Listen once without the transcript, then jot down every noun you caught and the general topic in one sentence
2. Shadowing exercise: Find any beginner dialogue clip and shadow these three lines, twice each, matching rhythm and pitch:
    おはようございます (ohayō gozaimasu, good morning)
    元気ですか (genki desu ka, how are you)
    また明日ね (mata ashita ne, see you tomorrow)
3. Dictation exercise: Play a 20-second NHK News Easy sentence that includes 台風 (taifū, typhoon). Write down the full sentence in kana, then double-check your particles. [...] The same rule applies to double consonants like きて (kite, come) versus きって (kitte, stamp). Train the ear by looping minimal pairs until the length difference feels obvious, not subtle.

### Match pitch and sentence flow

Japanese uses pitch accent, where the tone rises and falls across a word to signal meaning: 橋 (hashi, bridge) and 箸 (hashi, chopsticks) share the same syllables but follow different pitch patterns. Sentence-final particles like ね (ne) and よ (yo) also carry melody that shifts the whole feeling of what’s said.

Record yourself saying a sentence, then play the native version right after and listen for the shape of the pitch line. Fixing that curve in our own voice makes the same pattern easier to catch when a native speaker uses it at full speed. [...] ### Write dictation from short audio clips

Play a 10-15 second clip and write down every word you hear in かな (kana, syllabary) or 漢字 (kanji, Chinese characters). This forces us to notice the small pieces we usually skim past at natural speed.

Tip: Double-check かな (kana, syllabary) spelling and the little particles like は (wa, topic marker) and が (ga, subject marker) – they’re easy to miss but they change meaning.

### Fill in missing words from a transcript

Take a transcript, blank out 5-10 key words, then listen and fill them in. This drill trains focused attention without the pressure of catching every syllable.

Tip: NHK News Easy sentences work well as starters because they already include 振り仮名 (furigana, small kana above kanji to show pronunciation).

Who should pick this: Budget-conscious learners willing to invest setup time. People following textbooks who want to create custom flashcards. Anyone who values control over convenience. If you want a free alternative to Duolingo for Japanese and have the patience for it, Anki is unbeatable.

For learners who want the custom deck functionality but wrapped in actual gameplay, Lingo Legend’s CSV import feature lets you import your own study material into RPG and farm-sim modes.

### 6. Pimsleur

Best for: Speaking and listening practice, especially for commuters [...] Who should pick this: Absolute beginners mastering kana, or any learner wanting free JLPT kanji recognition practice. A zero-risk addition to any study stack.

## How to Build Your Japanese App Stack

Here’s something the Reddit community understands that most “best app” articles miss: no single app will teach you Japanese. The most successful learners stack tools, picking one for each core skill.

Analysis of r/LearnJapanese recommendations shows a clear pattern. The community’s most-suggested beginner combination is WaniKani for kanji, Bunpro for grammar, and Anki or a gamified alternative for vocabulary. Intermediate learners typically add Satori Reader for reading practice and YouTube or podcasts for listening.

### Beginner Stack (Just Starting Out) [...] Key features:

 Unlimited customization: add audio, images, furigana, example sentences
 Thousands of community-created Japanese decks
 Available on Windows, Mac, Linux, Android (free), and iOS ($25)
 Sync across devices via AnkiWeb
 Complete control over card intervals, design, and study parameters

Pricing: Free on desktop and Android. $25 one-time on iOS. No subscriptions.

Tradeoffs:

 Steep learning curve for setup and configuration
 Dated interface that hasn’t aged well
 No guided curriculum, lessons, or structure
 Requires self-discipline to create and maintain decks
 Not fun. At all.
